```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)
```

#First example
Daria's analysis of Aleksandr Dugin, "Putin's Brain"
```{r}
dugin <- read_csv("dugin_articles_df.csv") |> 
  clean_names()

```
# classify sentences by Putin
AI Gemini assisted with this code
```{r}
dugin1 <- dugin %>% 
  mutate(category = case_when(str_detect(sentence, regex("Putin", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Putin",
                              str_detect(sentence, "fascist") ~ "polarized_term",
                                str_detect(sentence, "brain") ~ "polarized_term",
                                                     TRUE~ "")) 
```


# Revised so it will capture Putin and fascist in a sentence
Checks each term independently
AI Gemini assisted with this code. See prompt below
```{r}
dugin <- dugin |> 
  mutate(
    # Check each condition independently
    has_putin = if_else(str_detect(sentence, regex("Putin", ignore_case = TRUE)), "Putin", NA_character_),
    has_polar = if_else(str_detect(sentence, regex("fascist|beard|brain", ignore_case = TRUE)), "polarized_term", NA_character_)
  ) %>%
  # Combine non-NA terms into a single string separated by commas
  unite("category", has_putin, has_polar, sep = ", ", na.rm = TRUE)
```


## Content analysis!

```{r}
dugin |> 
  count(category)


```

#Second example

```{r}
#import df created from sequence below

lynch <- read.csv("articles_oct_19.csv")
```

#### Categorize decades

```{r}
lynch_decade <- lynch %>% 
  mutate(decade = case_when(
         year < 1870 ~ "pre1870",
        year >= 1870 & year <=1879 ~ "1870s",
         year >= 1880 & year <=1889 ~ "1880s",
         year >= 1890 & year <=1899 ~ "1890s",
        year >= 1900 & year <=1909 ~ "1900s",
        year >= 1910 & year <=1919 ~ "1910s",
        year >= 1920 & year <=1929 ~ "1920s",
        year >= 1930 ~ "post1930s"
         ))

```


# Content analysis - count the decades

```{r}
lynch_decade |> 
  count(decade)


```

# Visualize by Region

```{r}
       subtitle = "Newspapers from Chronicling America, LOC",

```




#AI Gemini prompt:

i want to make sure if Putin and fascist are in the same article that they will both display in the category column separated by a comma. not sure this will do that.
dugin1<- dugin %>% 
  mutate(category = case_when(str_detect(sentence, regex("Putin", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Putin",
                              str_detect(sentence, "fascist") ~ "polarized_term",
                                str_detect(sentence, "beard") ~ "polarized_term",
                                                     TRUE~ ""))  
                                                     
#Response
You are correct—case_when() will not work for this because it stops evaluating as soon as it finds its first TRUE condition. If a sentence contains both "Putin" and "fascist", case_when() will only assign "Putin" and skip the rest.

To capture multiple non-exclusive conditions and combine them into a comma-separated list, you can check each condition separately and combine the results using c_across() and unite(), or construct a helper vector.

Here are the best ways to achieve this in standard dplyr / stringr:

Option 1: Clean & Standard dplyr Approach (Recommended)
You can build a small inline helper or combine logical evaluations into a list/vector, then paste them together.

R
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(tidyr)

dugin1 <- dugin %>%
  mutate(
    # Check each condition independently
    has_putin = if_else(str_detect(sentence, regex("Putin", ignore_case = TRUE)), "Putin", NA_character_),
    has_polar = if_else(str_detect(sentence, regex("fascist|beard", ignore_case = TRUE)), "polarized_term", NA_character_)
  ) %>%
  # Combine non-NA terms into a single string separated by commas
  unite("category", has_putin, has_polar, sep = ", ", na.rm = TRUE)
How it works:

If both match, category becomes "Putin, polarized_term".

If only one matches, category is just "Putin" or "polarized_term".

If neither matches, na.rm = TRUE leaves category as an empty string "".
